PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the operational framing that Colleagues 13, 14 and 15 are laying out is the one that actually maps onto how the blot is read in practice.

Western identity on a denaturing gel is antibody identity × apparent Mr. That second dimension only de-convolutes isoforms that live inside the same immunologic channel. Within a gene family it works very well because the N-terminal variants share the C-terminal catalytic/ADD epitope.

DNMT3A1 ~102–130 kDa and DNMT3A2 ~88–96 kDa are identical from the ADD/catalytic region onward, so a C-terminal pan-DNMT3A reagent gives two DNMT3A-positive bands assigned by size inside the DNMT3A channel: AbA high = A1, AbA low = A2. The same logic holds for DNMT3B: DNMT3B1 ~96 kDa and DNMT3B3 share the C-terminal catalytic/ADD core, so a C-terminal pan-DNMT3B reagent gives AbB high = B1 and AbB low = B3, with B3 reported in the literature as ~70–86 kDa and in some annotations as ~43–45 kDa.

DNMT3L is a separate catalytically inactive ~38–43 kDa paralog with essentially no DNMT3A/B catalytic domain homology in the reagents that are used routinely. It is not seen by conventional pan-DNMT3A or pan-DNMT3B catalytic reagents and it needs its own immunologic code.

The problem for a collapsed pan-DNMT3A/B code is family-isolated size. DNMT3A2 ~88–96 kDa essentially co-migrates with DNMT3B1 ~96 kDa on a standard 6–8% SDS gel, so a single pan-A/B blot gives an ~96 kDa immunoreactive band that cannot be assigned to A2 versus B1 by Mr alone. At the low Mr end the ambiguity is worse: DNMT3L ~43 kDa overlaps the literature range quoted for the most truncated DNMT3B3 forms, and the known ADD homology between DNMT3L and DNMT3B creates a real cross-reactivity risk for any truly pan-A/B reagent.

In practice there is no routinely validated clean commercial pan-DNMT3A/B catalytic antibody with assured DNMT3L segregation, and the published Mr heterogeneity for B3 makes a size-only de-convolution unreliable. Keeping the families immunologically segregated removes that assignment ambiguity.

Hence the minimum that gives five unique antibody × Mr signatures with reagents that are actually used is:

* pan-DNMT3A C-terminal → A1 high Mr, A2 low Mr
* pan-DNMT3B C-terminal → B1 high Mr, B3 low Mr  
* DNMT3L specific → L ~43 kDa

AbA high = DNMT3A1, AbA low = DNMT3A2, AbB high = DNMT3B1, AbB low = DNMT3B3, AbL = DNMT3L.

That is three independent immunodetections. 

The formal information-theoretic lower bound of a perfect pan-DNMT3A/B catalytic reagent plus DNMT3L, i.e. two immunologic codes, is a useful idealisation, and a single universal pan-A/B/L reagent would be the absolute theoretical limit. Those limits require perfect pan specificity with no DNMT3L cross-reactivity and perfect size separation of A2 vs B1 and B3 vs L. The A2/B1 ~96 kDa collision and the B3/L ~43 kDa proximity together with the lack of a validated pan-A/B reagent mean that idealisation is not a reliable distinguishability criterion in real Western practice. Three family-specific antibodies is the operational minimum normally quoted and used.

I’m fully on board with the antibody × apparent Mr read-out that’s been laid out here, and with the family-segregated operational minimum it implies.

Within DNMT3A the C-terminal/ADD catalytic region is shared by DNMT3A1 ≈102–130 kDa and DNMT3A2 ≈88–96 kDa, so a C-terminal pan-DNMT3A reagent gives one immunologic channel with two size-resolved DNMT3A-positive bands: AbA high = DNMT3A1, AbA low = DNMT3A2.

Within DNMT3B the same logic holds for DNMT3B1 ≈96 kDa and DNMT3B3, N-terminally truncated but identical over the C-terminal catalytic/ADD core. A C-terminal pan-DNMT3B reagent gives AbB high = DNMT3B1 and AbB low = DNMT3B3, with the low-MW B3 signal reported in the literature as ~70–86 kDa and in some annotations as ~43–45 kDa.

DNMT3L is a separate ~38–43 kDa catalytically inactive paralog with essentially no DNMT3A/B catalytic domain homology in routine reagents. It is not seen by conventional pan-DNMT3A or pan-DNMT3B catalytic antibodies and needs its own immunologic code, AbL ≈43 kDa = DNMT3L.

That yields five unique antibody × Mr signatures with three independent, non-cross-reacting family reagents:

pan-DNMT3A C-term → DNMT3A1 high, DNMT3A2 low
pan-DNMT3B C-term → DNMT3B1 high, DNMT3B3 low
DNMT3L specific → DNMT3L

The reason a collapsed pan-DNMT3A/B code cannot be used operationally is the loss of family isolation of the size code. DNMT3A2 ≈88–96 kDa essentially co-migrates with DNMT3B1 ≈96 kDa on standard 6–8% SDS gels, so a single pan-A/B blot would give an ~96 kDa immunoreactive band that cannot be assigned to A2 versus B1 by Mr alone. At the low-MW end the ambiguity is worse: DNMT3L ≈43 kDa sits on top of the literature range quoted for the most truncated DNMT3B3 forms, and the known ADD homology between DNMT3L and DNMT3B creates a realistic cross-reactivity risk for any truly pan-DNMT3A/B reagent.

No routinely validated commercial truly pan-DNMT3A/B catalytic antibody with clean DNMT3L segregation is used for isoform assignment in practice; published workflows keep A and B families separate for exactly this reason. The formal information-theoretic lower bound of a perfect pan-DNMT3A/B reagent plus DNMT3L, and the absolute ideal of one universal pan-A/B/L reagent, requires perfect pan specificity and perfect size separation of A2 vs B1 and B3 vs L. Published Mr ranges and gel resolution falsify both requirements in real practice.

Hence the minimum that gives unambiguous, routinely reproducible assignment for DNMT3A1, DNMT3A2, DNMT3B1, DNMT3B3 and DNMT3L on Western blot is the three family reagents pan-DNMT3A, pan-DNMT3B and DNMT3L-specific.

I think the operational framing that Colleagues 13, 14 and 15 are laying out is the one that actually maps onto how the blot is read in practice.

Western identity on a denaturing gel is antibody identity × apparent Mr. That second dimension only de-convolutes isoforms that live inside the same immunologic channel. Within a gene family it works very well because the N-terminal variants share the C-terminal catalytic/ADD epitope.

DNMT3A1 ~102–130 kDa and DNMT3A2 ~88–96 kDa are identical from the ADD/catalytic region onward, so a C-terminal pan-DNMT3A reagent gives two DNMT3A-positive bands assigned by size inside the DNMT3A channel: AbA high = A1, AbA low = A2. The same logic holds for DNMT3B: DNMT3B1 ~96 kDa and DNMT3B3 share the C-terminal catalytic/ADD core, so a C-terminal pan-DNMT3B reagent gives AbB high = B1 and AbB low = B3, with B3 reported in the literature as ~70–86 kDa and in some annotations as ~43–45 kDa.

DNMT3L is a separate catalytically inactive ~38–43 kDa paralog with essentially no DNMT3A/B catalytic domain homology in the reagents that are used routinely. It is not seen by conventional pan-DNMT3A or pan-DNMT3B catalytic reagents and it needs its own immunologic code.

The problem for a collapsed pan-DNMT3A/B code is family-isolated size. DNMT3A2 ~88–96 kDa essentially co-migrates with DNMT3B1 ~96 kDa on a standard 6–8% SDS gel, so a single pan-A/B blot gives an ~96 kDa immunoreactive band that cannot be assigned to A2 versus B1 by Mr alone. At the low Mr end the ambiguity is worse: DNMT3L ~43 kDa overlaps the literature range quoted for the most truncated DNMT3B3 forms, and the known ADD homology between DNMT3L and DNMT3B creates a real cross-reactivity risk for any truly pan-A/B reagent.

In practice there is no routinely validated clean commercial pan-DNMT3A/B catalytic antibody with assured DNMT3L segregation, and the published Mr heterogeneity for B3 makes a size-only de-convolution unreliable. Keeping the families immunologically segregated removes that assignment ambiguity.

Hence the minimum that gives five unique antibody × Mr signatures with reagents that are actually used is:

* pan-DNMT3A C-terminal → A1 high Mr, A2 low Mr
* pan-DNMT3B C-terminal → B1 high Mr, B3 low Mr  
* DNMT3L specific → L ~43 kDa

AbA high = DNMT3A1, AbA low = DNMT3A2, AbB high = DNMT3B1, AbB low = DNMT3B3, AbL = DNMT3L.

That is three independent immunodetections. 

The formal information-theoretic lower bound of a perfect pan-DNMT3A/B catalytic reagent plus DNMT3L, i.e. two immunologic codes, is a useful idealisation, and a single universal pan-A/B/L reagent would be the absolute theoretical limit. Those limits require perfect pan specificity with no DNMT3L cross-reactivity and perfect size separation of A2 vs B1 and B3 vs L. The A2/B1 ~96 kDa collision and the B3/L ~43 kDa proximity together with the lack of a validated pan-A/B reagent mean that idealisation is not a reliable distinguishability criterion in real Western practice. Three family-specific antibodies is the operational minimum normally quoted and used.

Operational non-cross-reacting laboratory scheme consensus across rounds:
* Ab A pan-DNMT3A C-term → A1 high MW, A2 low MW
* Ab B pan-DNMT3B C-term → B1 high MW, B3 low MW
* Ab L DNMT3L specific → L ~43 kDa
= three independent immunodetections giving five unique antibody × Mr signatures.

Key practical caveats repeatedly reinforced in round 4:
* A2 ~96 kDa essentially co-migrates with B1 ~96 kDa on standard 6-8% gels. A single pan-A/B immunochemical code cannot assign the ~96 kDa band to A2 vs B1 by Mr alone.

* Strictly isoform-unique epitope detection without size de-convolution would require five distinct antibodies.

Theoretical mathematical minimum = 2 reagents pan-A/B + DNMT3L, 1 reagent in ideal universal limit.
